Each fall, the Roger Ebert Fellowship program selects three College of Media undergraduate students at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to participate in a yearlong fellowship that aims to shape their skills in critical writing through immersion in the film industry. The Roger Ebert Fellows for the 2026-27 academic year are media and cinema studies students Ciel Baptiste, Ali Kilmek, and Kris Modi. This festival dispatch from the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival was authored by Baptiste, who attended screenings and events in their capacity as a fellow.
p

In the summer of 1972, documentarian William Greaves sent party invitations to individuals he identified as “luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance”—the explosive movement centered on Black artists, writers, and intellectuals in Harlem throughout the 1920s and 1930s—to document the get-together on film. What followed was perhaps the last gathering of its kind, a historic convergence of Black artistic lives that—with Greaves present to capture it on film for posterity—also marked one of the most important acts of cultural preservation since the Harlem Renaissance itself.
p

Greaves previously filmed the landmark documentary “Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One” in 1968, a wildly imaginative work that questions the director’s pedagogical role as it follows tensions between Greaves and his documentary crew. Given a dull, poorly written series of screen tests to film over the course of a week, the crew, having not read Greaves’ logline before taking the job, ends up filming their own efforts to gain control of the production. In true Greavesian fashion, this can be interpreted as an allegory for grassroots activism and the power of the people to create our own narratives.
p

Since 1953, Greaves had moved across genres and media, producing self-reflexive documentaries on Black history and culture; he also produced the monumentally important national news program “Black Journal,” which launched in 1968 and aired until 2008. In other words, he had established himself as a preeminent artist in his own right—and earned entry into the salons of the Harlem Renaissance’s surviving cadre.
p

Greaves’ voice and accompanying handwriting (further evidence of his well-preserved archives) inaugurate the film with a manifesto: “I propose to create a series of great films on great people, all of whom are metaphors, creations of the Godhead.” 50 years in the making, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” is a legendary assemblage of archival footage; it is also an incredibly intimate film, its cameras meandering through amicable dissensions and disputations between those great people, stopping by the punch bowl every so often for a refreshment.
p

At first, the writers and artists in attendance—gathered, notably, at Duke Ellington’s Harlem townhouse—reacquaint themselves, asking each other where their careers have led them over the preceding decades. However, they quickly settle in, soon moving to heavier matters of discourse. The Harlem Renaissance remains, to this day, a contested era: even its participants cannot agree on when it began and ended, whether it was a rebirth or an awakening, or whether it was a success or a failure (if its success can indeed be measured). Instead of tense disagreements, though, our Renaissance men and women remain engaged in earnest, careful dialogue.
p

“Harlem” values listening as much as debate; much of the film consists of shifting body language, quiet displays of camaraderie and kinship, disagreement, and annoyance. Greaves’ poetry, which closes out the film, ponders the collaborative nature of creativity: “It is an ancient paradox that, when one individual expresses himself, when he freely speaks and acts from the very privacy of his being, he reflects the thoughts and actions of many of his fellow men.” The art of discourse—and the collaborative explication of culture, memory, and meaning—rests at the heart of this film.
p

“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” is, at times, reminiscent of George Nierenberg’s effervescent (and criminally overlooked) gospel documentary “Say Amen, Somebody” from 1982; both films are documentaries of the 16mm-verité variety, observing historically important Black cultural movements as flies on the wall, looking into their legacies while the rest of the world moved on. Both are replete with delightfully retro color palettes and immaculately-restored photographs of their subjects’ younger days; while “Harlem” presents and preserves the titans of the Harlem Renaissance through innovative split-screen close-ups (à la “Symbiopsychotaxiplasm”), “Say Amen” chronicles the aging dignitaries of gospel through 24-track sound and agile camera work.
p

Preservation of Black history and culture through intergenerational conversation provides the foundation for both documentaries; just as the gospel music in “Say Amen” is inherently collaborative, with its choruses, audiences, and bandleaders blending together into one performing body, “Harlem” effaces the boundaries between its Renaissance personages, its documentary crew, and us as audience members.
p

I was lucky enough to catch a sold-out screening of “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” at the Chicago International Film Festival, which was presented by David and Liani Greaves, William’s son and granddaughter. Experiencing the film in this setting, I became aware that its emphasis on listening—and, in doing so, reaching deeper understanding—extended to those of us in the audience, too: the film subtly guides us to heed and use what we learn. David Greaves explained during the post-film Q&A that the completed documentary “is a realization of my father’s dream, to bring the people of the Harlem Renaissance to you, now.”
p

Seen in this light, their film is a true result of multigenerational co-creation. David was a camera operator on the day of filming, and upon his father’s death, the then-unedited footage was bequeathed to the younger Greaves for proper stewardship. That air of collaborative meaning-making was infectious during my screening; this documentary truly brings the audience close, welcoming viewers’ own interpretations of what they see and hear on screen. Throughout the film, I felt I wanted to hold on to every second of rapid-fire conversation—that the memories and experiences shared by those at the salon were too precious to forget, too essential to my own life to lose.
p

This feeling of audience belonging came to a head when the conversations preserved within “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” turned to the looming loss of cultural memory, to the fears of those directly involved in the Harlem Renaissance that its flourishing might be forgotten after their lifetimes.
p

Our theater was filled with people of all ages and strata, from students to industry professionals, but there were plenty of shared moments of awareness between us; when William Patterson, revolutionary labor leader and activist, is documented in the film declaring to his peers that “the Renaissance will never end,” those in my audience sensed he was speaking more to us than to those in the room with him in 1972.
p

Hearty chuckles filled the theater when Ida Mae Cullen, widow of poet Countee Cullen, pointed her finger ever so assertively at the others in the room, demanding they talk more than they have been about Zora Neale Hurston—not because we felt that it was a funny ask for Cullen to make, but because we saw ourselves represented (or perhaps our relatives, friends, and neighbors) in how she advocated for her loved ones.
p

This brings us back to Greaves’ purpose in filming this historic gathering; we become aware while watching that—as Liani reflected during the Q&A—the film “asks us to mindfully pay attention to what we’re creating in every moment” and how we’re moving through the world, “whether in community with each other or across intergenerational dynamics”. It implores us to wonder where our creativity and power—as artists or audience members—come from, and how the past filters down to us in the present. “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” is built to welcome us into the conversation, offering priceless knowledge and experience to those curious enough to seek it out.
p

As David noted after the screening, his father “believed in the divinity inherent in everyone.” His footage, which David directed and assembled so carefully, speaks for—and to—all of us. William Greaves’ voice closes the film, too, accompanying footage of our now-familiar dignitaries saying their goodbyes and, for the last time, separating into the outside world. His poem, chosen by Liani for the film (or, more specifically, demanded, according to David), ends with a line that left many of us in the theater teary-eyed: “The treasured prize of our survival is the joy of self-expression; in all those unique thoughts and actions that each person has to tell himself and all the world: I live.”
p

This urge to claim “I live” is innate to all of us. The figures of the Harlem Renaissance understood the power of a collaborative space to foster resistance to oppression and, beyond that, as an environment for intellectual stimulation and co-creation. The film proclaims this boldly: Black culture—literature, poetry, visual and sonic arts—exists unapologetically to lift us all to greater heights intellectually, artistically, and socially.
p

Liberatory Black art has existed since time immemorial, and during our Q&A, David spoke of the “genius of ancient Africans” and the “music they brought to America in their heads.” Today, the onus is on all of us to ensure its continued triumph. Our added task is to preserve and document its history and present; to ensure our culture remains accessible, visible, and unrestrained as an instrument of beauty, education, and liberation.
p

Sharing a room with David and Liani Greaves was a wonderful experience. They are both clearly devoted to the teachings of William Greaves as an artist and intellectual; much of their film’s power rests in how we realize those same philosophies can still be ours, too. Just as I felt that the film ended too soon (who wouldn’t want to maneuver through such animated conversations for just a few more hours?), I wished to hear more from David and Liani.
p

Their underscoring of the film’s messages by invoking William’s personal philosophies felt especially significant in such a collaborative environment; the Q&A session, in this sense, felt like a return to those conversations in Ellington’s Harlem townhouse. As Liani said after the film, discussing the gathering’s synergistic nature: “You saw it in the innate explosion of the Renaissance in the 1920s, you saw that in the film, and you see that now—if we engage that part of ourselves.”
p

Greaves’ masterpiece echoes—in form and in content—the interactivity and community which gave rise to the Renaissance itself. That same sense of community still drives events like the Chicago International Film Festival, thriving on collaborative curiosity.
p

Liani described “Symbiopsychotaxiplasm” as her grandfather’s experiment in “controlled chaos.” He wanted to bring together creative minds so their natural interactions would dialectically forge the film’s message before Greaves had a chance to narrow it down himself. The essence of “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” builds upon this concept simply through the complexity of its subjects and the timelessness of their ideas. At the end of the film, when he spoke of “reflecting the thoughts and actions of our fellow men,” William Greaves meant more than just making art; our whole life experiences bear the fruits of learning from and listening to one another.
p

Sharing our histories, especially intergenerationally, also helps us learn about ourselves. At times, the film’s subjects engage in semantics—not because they felt the need to have the final say in their discussions, but because they were well aware of the lasting impact of their words. As artists and intellectuals, they knew someone else would eventually define narratives of the past and present, if not they themselves. “If I can’t publish something that helps us,” journalist Gerri Major testifies, “I’ll never publish something that hurts us.”
p

Perhaps that is why this film has taken so many decades to grace the silver screen. “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” at once a catalyst and a product of harmony and fellowship, invites us to go beyond a simple indulgence in curiosity about the past. It asks us to bring our ancestors with us into the present, not only to remember their struggles but to build on that work toward a better future for everyone. “The film continues with all of you,” Liani told us in her closing remarks. “We wanted the film to be a co-creation across time. We want people to take this collaborative experience, because it belongs to you.” And what a gift it is.
